questions.question: How does encapsulation work in Python?
questions.title: Encapsulation and Non-Public Names in Python
questions.direct_answer: Python encapsulation is mainly an API-design practice: an object keeps related state and behaviour together, exposes useful operations, marks implementation details with `_name`, and may use `__name` mangling to avoid subclass name clashes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Python's conventions instead of claiming it has Java-style private fields.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying double underscores make data secure or completely inaccessible from outside the class.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Separate non-public API convention, name mangling, and actual invariant protection through methods or properties.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Encapsulation keeps related state and operations behind a clear public API.
A leading underscore marks a name as non-public by convention.
A double-leading underscore triggers class-name mangling.
Name mangling prevents accidental subclass clashes; it is not access security.
Methods and properties can protect rules when state changes.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Encapsulation means keeping an object's state together with the operations that are allowed to change it, then exposing a small public interface. Python supports that design, but ordinary Python classes do not enforce completely private instance variables.

A name such as `_balance` says that callers should treat it as an implementation detail. A name such as `__token` is rewritten with the class name, for example `_Session__token`. That feature mainly prevents an accidental collision when a subclass chooses the same attribute name; determined code can still access it.

For example, a `BankAccount` can expose `deposit` and `withdraw` while storing `_balance`. The withdrawal method rejects a negative amount or an amount larger than the current balance. Callers use the operations instead of changing the number directly, so the object can preserve its rule.

Encapsulation is therefore about a dependable API rather than hiding data for security. A leading underscore communicates ownership, and a property or method controls reads and writes when validation is required. Double underscores should be reserved for avoiding subclass clashes, not used on every attribute.

sections.title: Protect the rule, not the spelling
sections.content:
A useful object has invariants: statements that should remain true after every public operation. An account balance may never fall below zero, or a temperature may never be stored below absolute zero. Encapsulation places the code responsible for that rule beside the state it protects.

Python's single-underscore convention tells people and tools that a name is not part of the stable public interface. This is social enforcement, but it is valuable: internal representation can change without promising compatibility. Two leading underscores activate name mangling inside a class definition. The rewritten name includes the defining class, making accidental overriding less likely in inheritance hierarchies.

Neither form encrypts or secures information. If a value is sensitive, access control belongs at the system boundary. Within a class, methods and properties provide a place to validate transitions. The best design usually exposes meaningful operations such as `withdraw`, not mechanical getters and setters for every field.

sections.title: What each naming form means
sections.content:
| Form | Typical meaning | Enforced privacy? | Main use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `balance` | Public API | No | Normal caller access |
| `_balance` | Non-public implementation detail | No | Signal that callers should not depend on it |
| `__balance` | Name-mangled to include the class | No | Avoid accidental name clashes in subclasses |
| `__balance__` | Special-method style | No | Reserved for Python-defined protocols, not private data |

sections.title: Expose an operation that preserves the invariant

questions.question: What is a property in Python, and why is it useful?
questions.title: Python Properties for Managed Attributes
questions.direct_answer: A property lets normal attribute syntax run getter, setter, or deleter logic. It is useful for validation, computed values, and changing an implementation without forcing callers to switch from `obj.name` to method calls.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can manage attribute access with Python's idiomatic property mechanism.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing Java-style `get_x` and `set_x` methods for simple fields or creating recursive property setters.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that the public name and backing attribute must be different and that a property is a descriptor.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `@property` makes a method readable with attribute syntax.
`@name.setter` can validate assignments to that public attribute.
A separate backing name such as `_price` prevents recursion.
A property can be read-only when no setter is defined.
Use plain public attributes until managed access provides real value.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A property is a managed attribute. It lets callers use natural syntax such as `product.price`, while Python runs a method when that name is read. An optional setter can run another method for `product.price = value`.

For example, a `Product` may store its number in `_price`. The `price` getter returns that value, and the setter rejects zero or negative prices before updating it. Callers see one stable attribute-style API, while the class controls the rule.

The backing attribute must have a different name. If the setter assigns `self.price = value`, it calls itself again and eventually raises `RecursionError`; assigning `self._price` stores the actual value. Leaving out the setter makes the public property read-only through normal assignment.

Properties are also useful for computed values and for evolving an earlier public attribute into managed behaviour without changing caller syntax. They are implemented through Python's descriptor protocol. I would not add properties mechanically to every field, because a plain public attribute is clearer when no validation, calculation, or compatibility boundary exists.

sections.title: Properties and controlled attribute access
sections.content:
Python code commonly begins with direct attribute access. Later, a rule may appear: values need validation, an old representation must be converted, or a result can be calculated from other fields. A property places this behaviour behind the same dot syntax, so users of the class do not need a new `get_...` call.

The decorated getter creates a descriptor on the class. Attribute lookup recognizes that descriptor and invokes its `__get__` behaviour. Adding a setter supplies the matching write path. The class normally keeps raw storage under a non-public backing name so the managed public name can remain free for the descriptor.

This mechanism is best for access that still feels like an attribute. A slow network request, a command with important side effects, or an operation that can fail for many business reasons is clearer as an explicitly named method. The syntax should help callers predict the cost and meaning.

sections.title: One public name, two controlled paths
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  W[product.price = 80] --> S[price setter validates 80]
  S --> B[store self._price]
  R[read product.price] --> G[price getter runs]
  G --> B
  B --> V[return stored value]
```

sections.title: Validate a price without changing caller syntax
